title: The month-end close is slow because work waits, not accountants
dek: Most close days are spent waiting for late inputs, approvals and rework, not on accounting work. Map the close as a dependency network and fix the flow before buying software or AI.
description: The month-end close is slow because work waits, not because accountants are slow. Map it as a dependency network and fix the flow before buying close tools.

title: AI agents rarely fail at the task. They fail at the hand-off
dek: Agent projects in services operations stall where work moves between the agent, people and systems. Design the hand-off before you design the agent.
description: AI agents in services operations rarely fail at the task. They stall at hand-offs. The evidence, and a checklist to design each hand-off before you build the agent.

title: Process drift: closing the gap between the SOP and the real work
dek: Every documented process drifts from how work is really done. Here is a step-by-step playbook to find the gap, sort good drift from bad, and close it on a fixed cadence.
description: A practical playbook for finding the gap between documented and real processes, classifying each variant, and closing it without monitoring what people write.

title: The cost of rework: the biggest line your P&L never shows
dek: Corrections, re-requests, returned files and write-offs add up to a cost most services firms never see as one number. Measure first pass yield by workflow, then price it.
description: Rework is the biggest cost most services firms never measure. How to track first pass yield by workflow and put a price on rework without monitoring individuals.

title: Automated decisions: Australia's 10 December privacy deadline
dek: From 10 December, Australian privacy policies must describe where software makes or shapes significant decisions about people. You cannot disclose what you have not mapped.
description: Australia's new privacy rule on automated decisions starts 10 December 2026. What it requires, how UK and US rules compare, and a practical readiness checklist.

title: Work about work is a hand-off problem, not a people problem
dek: Surveys keep finding that more than half the week goes on coordination. The cause is not individual habits. It is the hand-offs nobody designed.
description: Why 'work about work' takes more than half of the knowledge worker's week, why focus campaigns and new tools underdeliver, and how to measure the hand-offs where time really disappears.

title: Flow efficiency: the number that explains why simple work takes weeks
dek: The work takes hours. The case takes weeks. Little's Law and a little queuing theory explain the gap, and how to close it.
description: What flow efficiency is, why knowledge work often sits at 5 to 15 per cent, how Little's Law links open work to cycle time, and how services firms can measure and reduce waiting.

title: Why automation programs stall, and how to choose your first five
dek: From RPA to generative AI, most pilots never pay back. The problem is rarely the technology. It is what gets chosen for automation.
description: Why 30 to 50 per cent of RPA projects and most generative AI pilots fail to deliver, why automating non-bottleneck steps rarely pays, and five tests for choosing automations that do.

title: How to build an automation business case your CFO will sign
dek: Hours saved are not dollars saved. A structure for sizing automation that survives a sceptical finance team, with a worked example.
description: A practical method for automation ROI: measured volumes, automation rate, adoption ramps, risk adjustment and full-life costs, plus how to separate capacity released from cash realised.

title: How to map work without monitoring people
dek: Process discovery and employee surveillance are different things. Here is what the law says in Australia, the UK and the US, and the design principles that keep them apart.
description: Workplace surveillance and privacy law for process discovery in Australia (NSW, ACT, Victoria, Privacy Act), the UK (ICO guidance) and the US (New York, California), and seven privacy-first design principles.
